abstract.para: Whether a message comes from a plain-text file or from the journal, it follows a predictable structure and carries a priority level. Knowing both helps you find what matters quickly.

section.title: Anatomy of a plain-text log line
section.para: A line in a plain-text log file such as /var/log/messages consists of a time stamp, the host name, the name of the program that generated the message (usually followed by its process ID in brackets), and the message text itself:

example.title: A line from /var/log/messages
example.screen: 2026-09-07T09:21:30.439903+02:00 sles16 sshd-session[4731]: pam_unix(sshd:session): session opened for user tux(uid=1000) by tux(uid=0)

section.para: In this example, 2026-09-07T09:21:30.439903+02:00 is the time stamp (in ISO 8601 format, including the time zone offset), sles16 is the host name, sshd-session is the program that logged the message, 4731 is its process ID, and everything after the colon is the message itself. Not every program includes a process ID. Certain programs log under just their name.

section.title: Priority levels
section.para: Every log message carries a priority level indicating its severity. The same eight levels apply both to journal entries (visible in the PRIORITY field, and filterable with journalctl -p) and to the selector lines in rsyslog configuration files (for example, *.err or mail.warning), which decide into which file a message is written. Raw kernel messages, such as those in boot.msg or the output of dmesg, show the same level as a bracketed number prefix, for example, <6> for info.

row.entry: A service or application failed to complete a requested operation.
Something undesirable happened, but it is not a failure.

section.para: When troubleshooting, start by looking for the lowest-numbered (most severe) entries around the time the problem occurred, for example, with journalctl -p err -b. For details on querying the journal by priority, boot, or time range, see .
